isthmus.label: supported
isthmus.says: Corinth was a city-state on the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow neck of land joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece.
quote: was a city-state (polis) on the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow stretch of land that joins the Peloponnese peninsula to mainland Greece

big.label: estimate
big.says: Ancient Corinth was one of the largest and most important cities of Greece, with an estimated population of about 90,000 in 400 BC.
quote: Ancient Corinth was one of the largest and most important cities of Greece, with a population of 90,000 in 400 BC.

wealth.label: supported
wealth.says: Corinthians were wealthy because all land traffic to the Peloponnese passed through the isthmus.
quote: The Corinthians were also known for their wealth due to their strategic location on the isthmus, through which all land traffic had to pass en route to the Peloponnese

roman.label: supported
roman.says: Rome demolished Corinth in 146 BC, built a new city in 44 BC, and later made it the capital of the province of Achaea.
quote: The Romans demolished Corinth in 146 BC after they captured it as result of the Battle of Corinth, built a new city in its place in 44 BC, and later made it the provincial capital of Achaea.

caesar.label: supported

mixed.label: supported

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: Inside the site, at a spot where you can see the old columns of the Temple of Apollo on their rocky rise.

paras.t: Welcome to Ancient Corinth. It grew rich on the Isthmus, the narrow neck of land joining southern Greece to the mainland, where all land traffic had to pass.
There's little shade here. Keep your hat on, drink often, and watch your step on the old paving.

In its prime it was one of the largest cities in Greece, with an estimated population of about 90,000 in 400 BC. Then, in 146 BC, the Romans destroyed it. It lay largely deserted until Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, and Rome later made it the capital of the province of Achaea.
So the city Paul walked into was a Roman one, and a crowded one. Romans, Greeks and Jews lived side by side.
American archaeologists have been digging here since 1896. They can't dig everywhere, though: the modern village of Ancient Corinth sits right on top of the old city.

parts.name: The Temple of Apollo
parts.stand: Walk toward the temple and stop where you can see all of its standing columns.

paras.t: Up on the rocky hill stand seven columns of the Temple of Apollo, built in the middle of the 500s BC. It's one of the earliest Doric temples in Greece.

It's also one of the few things here that never disappeared from view. And it had several lives. The Romans restored it for the worship of the emperor. In Byzantine times it became a church. Under the Ottomans part of it was pulled down, and the local Bey built a house on top of its base.

Somewhere near the temple is the Glauke Fountain, said to have been built in Roman times. As the story goes, Glauke was about to marry Jason, the hero of the Argonauts, when Medea sent her a poisoned robe. It burst into flames, and she threw herself into the fountain that now carries her name.

parts.name: Paul comes to Corinth
parts.stand: Walk on into the remains of the Roman city and find a spot to stop.

paras.t: Now to the reason many people come here. The book of Acts, chapter eighteen, begins: "After these things Paul departed from Athens, and came to Corinth."
He moved in with a couple, Aquila and Priscilla, and Acts says why: "for by their occupation they were tentmakers." So was he.

Aquila was a Jew, lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. In the words of Acts: "because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought."
Think about that for a moment. The apostle earned his keep with his hands, working alongside new friends. That's where the modern Christian idea of "tentmaking" gets its name.

Every sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue. When Silas and Timotheus came down from Macedonia and he was opposed, he said: "from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles." He went next door, into the house of a man named Justus, "whose house joined hard to the synagogue." And Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, believed, with all his house.

Then, Acts says, the Lord spoke to Paul in the night by a vision: "Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace: For I am with thee, and no man shall set on thee to hurt thee: for I have much people in this city."

So he stayed, Acts says, "a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them." Historians place that first visit around AD 49 or 50. Christian tradition counts Corinth as a church founded by an apostle, by Paul himself.
Acts tells of one dramatic day here. "When Gallio was the deputy of Achaia," Paul's opponents "brought him to the judgment seat."

Gallio was the Roman governor, the brother of the philosopher Seneca. The charge was that Paul persuaded men to worship God contrary to the law. When Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio would not hear it. His answer ended: "But if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of such matters." And he drove them from the judgment seat.
It got ugly. The Greeks took Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, and beat him right in front of the judgment seat. And Acts adds, dryly: "Gallio cared for none of those things."

Where was that judgment seat? Among the important monuments of this site is one called the Bema, which later became a church of the Apostle Paul. We don't know whether Paul stood on this very spot, so that question is yours to ponder.
Gallio isn't only a name in the Bible. Historians date the trial to AD 51 or 52, and an inscription that mentions the Roman proconsul Gallio is on display in the museum at Delphi.

parts.name: Letters to Corinth
parts.stand: Find a bit of shade nearby and take a breather.

paras.t: Paul stayed a good while longer. Then he sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. Acts adds a small detail: "having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow." Cenchreae was Corinth's harbor on the Saronic Gulf, to the east.

He didn't forget this city. He wrote at least two letters to the church here, First and Second Corinthians, and he came back. He stayed again for about three months, and it is believed he wrote his letter to the Romans here.
From his first letter to the Christians of this city, in the King James Version: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity."
A few lines earlier in the same chapter: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up."

parts.name: Acrocorinth, the hill above
parts.stand: Look up at the great rock that towers over the site.

paras.t: That huge rock above us is Acrocorinth, Upper Corinth, the city's acropolis. The scholar George Forrest called it the most impressive acropolis of mainland Greece.
If you go up, the climb is steep and shadeless. Go early or late on a hot day, wear good shoes, and carry water.

It had its own water supply and it commanded the Isthmus, so it became a last line of defense for southern Greece. People lived up there from archaic times into the early 1800s. Three rings of walls defended it. The Byzantines fortified it heavily, and later Franks, Venetians and Ottomans all held it. From 1205 the Corinthians held out up there against the crusaders, at first under Leo Sgouros. The rock did not fall until 1210.
On the highest peak stood a temple to Aphrodite. It became a church, and later a mosque.

The Corinthians had myths for this rock too. In one, a being called Briareus settled a quarrel between the gods: the Isthmus went to Poseidon, god of the sea, and this rock to Helios, the sun. And legend says the winged horse Pegasus drank at the Upper Peirene spring, inside the walls, where the hero Bellerophon caught and tamed him.

One last thought. Acts tells of three tentmakers and a house next door to the synagogue. Not much, next to a fortress like that. Yet the words written to the people of this city are still read today, far beyond it.
